summary: Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest paths from one source vertex to every other vertex in a graph whose edge weights are non-negative. It repeatedly finalizes the closest unfinalized vertex and relaxes its outgoing edges.

sections.heading: Idea
sections.body: Keep a tentative distance dist[v] for every vertex, initially infinity except dist[source] = 0. At each step pick the unfinalized vertex u with the smallest dist, declare it final (its shortest path is now known), and try to improve its neighbours: if dist[u] + w(u, v) < dist[v], update dist[v]. This is the greedy choice: with non-negative weights no later path can reach u more cheaply.

sections.heading: Array version, O(V²)
sections.body: Simple and best for dense graphs. A 0 in the matrix means no edge.

sections.heading: Priority-queue version
sections.body: Store (distance, vertex) pairs in a min-heap. Pop the smallest; skip it if it is stale (larger than the current dist). Relax edges and push improved neighbours. With adjacency lists the total time is O((V + E) log V).

sections.heading: Complexity
bullets: Array: O(V²) time, O(V) extra space.
Binary heap + adjacency lists: O((V + E) log V).
Fibonacci heap: O(E + V log V) in theory.
Space: O(V + E) for the graph.

sections.heading: Negative edges
sections.body: Dijkstra's correctness relies on a finalized vertex never being improved later. A negative edge could make a path through an unfinalized vertex cheaper, so the answer would be wrong. Use Bellman-Ford (O(VE)) when negative weights exist.

Edges: A-B 4, A-C 2, C-B 1, B-D 5, C-D 8. Start dist = {A:0}. Finalize A: B=4, C=2. Finalize C (2): B improves to 3, D=10. Finalize B (3): D improves to 8. Finalize D. Final: A0, C2, B3, D8; path to D is A -> C -> B -> D.
Whenever you improve dist[v] through u, set parent[v] = u. After the run, follow parents from the target back to the source and reverse the list.

If you need only one destination, stop when it is popped. A* adds a heuristic estimate of remaining distance to the priority, expanding fewer vertices while staying optimal for admissible heuristics (used in maps and games).

bullets: Bellman-Ford: negative edges and negative-cycle detection, O(VE).
Network routing: OSPF runs Dijkstra on the link-state database.

takeaways: Greedy: repeatedly finalize the closest unfinalized vertex and relax its edges.
O(V²) with arrays, O((V+E) log V) with a heap.
Track parents to rebuild the actual path.
